prompt: `load.py` passed ids, documents and metadata to `col.add`, and no vectors. Where did the 40 vectors come from?
hint: Look at what `same.py` compared.

choices.text: Chroma ran its default embedding function on the texts
choices.why: Right. With no `embeddings` argument, Chroma embeds the documents itself, and `same.py` found its stored vector equal to `minilm.embed`'s to the eighth decimal.

choices.text: Chroma kept only the texts and makes a vector each time a query arrives
choices.why: The vectors are made when the records are written: `same.py` read a stored vector back with `include=["embeddings"]`.

choices.text: Chroma sent the texts to labembed, the lab's stand-in provider
choices.why: The default embedding function runs an ONNX file inside the Python process; nothing in `load.py` talks to port 8500.

choices.text: Chroma hashed each text into 384 numbers
choices.why: A hash would not land within 3.7e-08 of the model's vector. The numbers came from the model.

prompt: `same.py` compared Chroma's stored vector for h15 with `minilm.embed` of the same text and found a largest difference of about 3.7e-08. What does that show?
hint: Where did `minilm.py` get its model file?

choices.text: Chroma compresses vectors a little when it stores them
choices.why: A compressed vector would differ far more than in the eighth decimal, and the stored array had all 384 numbers in float32.

choices.text: Both are the same model, and the gap is rounding
choices.why: Right. `minilm.py` runs Chroma's own ONNX export, so the only difference is two programs doing the same arithmetic in a slightly different order.

choices.text: They are different models that happen to agree closely
choices.why: Two different models give unrelated coordinates, as lesson 1 showed; agreement to the eighth decimal is the same model.

choices.text: Chroma normalises the vector and `minilm.py` does not
choices.why: Both return unit-length vectors. Normalising one and not the other would change every number, not the eighth decimal.

prompt: A nightly job re-imports the help centre into Chroma with `col.add`, using the article ids. An article was edited yesterday. What does the collection hold for it after tonight's run?
hint: `change.py` called `add` twice with the same id.

choices.text: The edited text, because `add` replaces a record with the same id
choices.why: That is what `upsert` does. `change.py`'s second `add` left 'Gift cards by email.' in place.

choices.text: The old text and its old vector, and no error was raised
choices.why: Right. `add` with an existing id changes nothing and says nothing, so the job keeps the first version of every article for ever.

choices.text: Both versions, under the same id
choices.why: The count stayed at 41 after the second `add`: one record per id.

choices.text: Nothing for that article, because the import stops with a duplicate-id error
choices.why: No error was raised; the program carried on to the `upsert` line.

prompt: `dims.py` queried the collection with a 256-number WordLlama vector and Chroma refused. What would happen with a vector from another model that also returns 384 numbers?
hint: What exactly did the error message compare?

choices.text: Chroma would refuse, because it records which model made the collection
choices.why: The check is the dimension: 'expecting embedding with dimension of 384, got 256'. Another 384-number vector passes it.

choices.text: Chroma would convert the vector into the collection's model first
choices.why: There is no conversion between models; their coordinates have nothing to do with each other.

choices.text: Chroma would answer, and the ranking would mean nothing
choices.why: Right. The size matches, so the query runs, but the two models' coordinates are unrelated, as lesson 1 warned. The database cannot tell.

choices.text: Chroma would answer correctly, since both have 384 dimensions
choices.why: Equal dimension does not make two models comparable; lesson 1 said so of any two models.

prompt: To insert a record when its id is new and overwrite it when the id already exists, call Chroma's ___ method.
hint: `change.py` used it after the second `add` failed to change anything.

prompt: Marginalia wants a backup of the help-centre collection kept with `PersistentClient`. What does it need to copy, while nothing is writing?
hint: Where did the listing find the files?

choices.text: The `chroma` directory
choices.why: Right. The directory is the whole database: the SQLite file and the index directory beside it.

choices.text: `chroma.sqlite3` on its own
choices.why: The index lives in the directory beside it, named by the segment's id; copying one file leaves the other behind.

choices.text: An export of the vectors, since the texts can be rebuilt from them
choices.why: A vector cannot be read back as its text. The documents are stored separately, in the SQLite file.

choices.text: Nothing, since Chroma keeps a copy on its own servers
choices.why: `PersistentClient` has no server; the directory on Marginalia's disk is the only copy.

prompt: `inside.py` counted 160 rows in `embedding_metadata` for 40 records with three metadata keys each. How many rows would 100 records with five metadata keys each give, with the document stored the same way?
hint: The document is stored as one more key.

prompt: `embeddings_queue` had 45 rows after `load.py` and `change.py`. Why 45 and not 40?
hint: Read the last five rows `inside.py` printed.

choices.text: It keeps one row per version of each record, and h41 had five versions
choices.why: h41 had two texts, and two of the five rows are not h41's changes at all: one is the ignored `add`, one is the `update` of h99.

choices.text: Deleted records stay in it as five markers
choices.why: Only one of the five rows is a delete. The others are two adds, an upsert and an update.

choices.text: It counts one row per article plus one per category
choices.why: There are six categories, which would make 46, and the rows `inside.py` printed name writes, not categories.

choices.text: It logs each write call, and `change.py` made five, including two that changed nothing
choices.why: Right. The 40 adds of `load.py` and the add, add, upsert, update and delete of `change.py`, each recorded like any other write.

prompt: In `grow.py`, `data_level0.bin` was 167,600 bytes at 40 records and still 167,600 at 940. A colleague concludes that 900 records were lost. What would you tell them?
hint: Look at the line `grow.py` printed first.

choices.text: They were lost, and only a restart would bring them back
choices.why: `col.count()` printed 940, which Chroma could not report for records it had lost.

choices.text: In the write log; the index files wait for 1,000 writes
choices.why: Right. `sync_threshold` is 1,000, and the file changed between 940 and 1,040 records. The file's size says nothing about the count.

choices.text: They were stored in a second index directory the listing did not show
choices.why: `grow` held one collection and one segment directory; the growth arrived in the same file at 1,040.

choices.text: They fit in the empty slots, since the file had room for a hundred records
choices.why: A hundred slots cannot hold 940 records; the file was simply not rewritten until the threshold.

prompt: With `chroma run` serving the directory, `remote.py` passed `query_texts`. Which program turned the question into a vector?
hint: Where does the Python client's embedding function run?

choices.text: The `chroma run` server, which loaded all-MiniLM-L6-v2
choices.why: The server never loaded a model: the Python client embeds before it sends anything.

choices.text: `remote.py` itself, through the collection's embedding function
choices.why: Right. The client runs the embedding function, and the question crossed the network as 384 numbers.

choices.text: labembed, on port 8500
choices.why: Nothing in `remote.py` or the collection points at labembed; Chroma's default function runs in-process.

choices.text: No program: the server searched the text with its full-text table
choices.why: The answers came with distances, which a full-text match does not produce; it was a vector search.

prompt: A team tested `distance < 0.6` on a cosine collection, then ran the same code against a collection created with no configuration. Search now returns nothing, and nothing errors. Why?
hint: What is the default space, and where did h18 land in it?

choices.text: The new collection's index is still being built
choices.why: A collection answers as soon as records are added; `distances.py` queried its new ones immediately.

choices.text: The new collection used a different embedding model
choices.why: Even with the same vectors, as in `distances.py`, the numbers change: the space changed, not the model.

choices.text: The default space is squared L2, where the best article sat at 1.1089
choices.why: Right. `l2` gives 2 − 2 × similarity, so the same articles sit above 1, and a cut-off of 0.6 keeps none of them.

choices.text: The default space returns similarities, so the comparison must be reversed
choices.why: The default `l2` returns a distance too, smaller is closer; only the scale differs.

prompt: Why did `distances.py` create two new collections instead of switching `help` to another space?
hint: What did `space.py` try?

choices.text: Chroma allows one space per directory
choices.why: One directory held `help`, `help_l2` and `help_ip`, in three spaces.

choices.text: The space can be changed only while the collection is empty
choices.why: `modify` does not accept `space` at all; the error listed the fields it does accept.

choices.text: Changing the space would delete the documents
choices.why: There was no change to make: Chroma refused before anything happened.

choices.text: A collection's space is fixed when it is created
choices.why: Right. `space.py`'s `modify` was refused, and the field list omitted `space`. Another space means another collection.

prompt: Two unit vectors have a dot product of 0.30. What distance does a Chroma collection created with no configuration return between them?
hint: The default space is `l2`, and it is squared.

prompt: Marginalia's help collection was created in the `l2` space and has to measure cosine instead. Put the steps in order.
hint: The old collection is the last thing to go.
items: Create a new collection with the cosine space
Add every record's id, document, metadata and vector to it
Point the search code at the new collection
trap: Deleting first leaves the search with nothing, and there is no `modify` that changes a space in place.

prompt: In `pine.py`, what does a namespace do?
hint: The English and Portuguese articles went to different places in one index.

choices.text: Sets the region where the index is stored
choices.why: The region is in `ServerlessSpec`, chosen once for the whole index.

choices.text: Partitions one index, so a query sees only the namespace it names
choices.why: Right. `en` and `pt` are two partitions of `help`, and a query names exactly one.

choices.text: Names the embedding model that the index uses
choices.why: `pine.py` embeds the texts itself; a namespace says nothing about a model.

choices.text: Lists the metadata keys a filter is allowed to read
choices.why: Filters read the metadata of each record; the namespace decides which records are searched at all.

prompt: Marginalia moves its search from a Chroma cosine collection to a Pinecone cosine index and keeps the rule 'show an article when its number is below 0.6'. What goes wrong?
hint: Which way does Pinecone's number point?

choices.text: Nothing, since both use cosine and return the same numbers
choices.why: Chroma returns 1 − similarity and Pinecone the similarity itself; the same metric, opposite conventions.

choices.text: Pinecone's numbers run from 0 to 2, so the rule lets too few through
choices.why: That is the range of Chroma's cosine distance. Pinecone's cosine score is a similarity, highest for the closest.

choices.text: It is a similarity there, so the rule now keeps the weakest matches
choices.why: Right. For a cosine index the best match has the highest score, so the old rule selects the articles furthest from the question.

choices.text: Pinecone refuses thresholds and accepts only `top_k`
choices.why: The client returns each match's score; what you do with it afterwards is your program's choice.

prompt: In Pinecone, a partition inside one index that a query names, such as `en` in `pine.py`, is called a ___.
hint: The three Portuguese articles were upserted into another one.

prompt: What does `alpha=0.5` in Weaviate's `query.hybrid` ask for?
hint: 1 and 0 are the two pure searches.

choices.text: Only results closer than a distance of 0.5
choices.why: That would be a distance limit; `alpha` weighs two searches against each other.

choices.text: Half the results from the keyword list, half from the vector list
choices.why: The two lists are fused into one ranking, not taken in halves.

choices.text: Equal weight for the keyword search and the vector search
choices.why: Right. 1 is a pure vector search and 0 a pure keyword search; 0.5 weighs the two equally.

choices.text: A vector search over half the collection, chosen at random
choices.why: Nothing is sampled. `alpha` balances BM25 against the vector distance.

prompt: A Weaviate collection uses `Configure.Vectors.text2vec_openai(...)` instead of `self_provided`. What changes for Marginalia?
hint: Who calls the provider?

choices.text: Marginalia's program must send vectors with every query
choices.why: That is `self_provided`. With a vectorizer module a query can arrive as text through `near_text`.

choices.text: The server calls OpenAI for each insert and text query
choices.why: Right. The embedding moves to the server: it holds the provider's key and the provider bills each call.

choices.text: Weaviate stops using HNSW and searches by keyword
choices.why: The vectorizer only decides who makes the vectors; the vector index is configured separately.

choices.text: The vectors are computed once by Weaviate and never again
choices.why: Every inserted object and every text query is embedded by the module, so the calls continue.

prompt: Marginalia moves its help-centre search from `PersistentClient` to `chroma run` on a server. What becomes the team's job that was not before?
hint: `remote.py` used the same collection methods.

choices.text: Rewriting the search code for another API
choices.why: `remote.py` changed only the constructor; every collection call stayed the same.

choices.text: Choosing a new embedding model
choices.why: The client still runs the same default function; the model did not change.

choices.text: Keeping a server process running, upgraded, monitored and backed up
choices.why: Right. On a server you run, the process and its files are yours to operate.

choices.text: Paying Chroma for every query
choices.why: `chroma run` is open-source software on your machine; paying per use is the hosted shape.

hint: One place on the right is not where any model runs.

pairs.right: The Weaviate server calls a provider
Your code, before it sends the vectors

pairs.left: A Pinecone index with an integrated model

prompt: Marginalia is choosing where the vectors of its customers' messages will live: a Chroma directory or a hosted service. Which questions decide it? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think about who operates it and what leaves the building.

choices.text: Who will operate the database and be woken when it fails
choices.why: Yes. A directory is yours to run; a hosted service is the provider's.

choices.text: Whether these vectors may leave Marginalia's machines
choices.why: Yes. Lesson 1 said a message's vector is personal data like the message, so where it goes is a privacy question.

choices.text: How many programs must reach the data at once
choices.why: Yes. One program can own a directory; many programs need a server, yours or the provider's.

choices.text: Which of the two is faster on forty articles
choices.why: At forty articles there is nothing to measure; any of them, or NumPy, is fast enough.

choices.text: Whether the vectors are stored as float32
choices.why: All of them store numbers; the format does not decide where the database runs.

prompt: In a Chroma collection created with the cosine space, the number a query returns equals one minus the ___ of the two vectors.
hint: Lesson 1 called it a score.

prompt: Match each setting with what a query returns under it.
hint: Two of them give the same number for unit vectors.
right_distractors: The angle between the vectors in degrees

prompt: Marginalia serves its Chroma directory with `chroma run` and searches it from another program. Put the steps in order.
hint: The question becomes numbers before it travels.
items: Start chroma run with the path of the directory
Connect to it with HttpClient and get the collection
The client embeds the question with the collection's function
The server searches the index and returns ids and distances
trap: The server does not embed the question: the Python client does it before sending anything.

prompt: The three Portuguese articles must never appear for an English question in Pinecone, even if somebody forgets a filter. Which design does that?
hint: One of these needs every query to remember something.

choices.text: A metadata field lang set to pt, and a filter on it in each query
choices.why: That works only while every query carries the filter; one query without it sees all the articles.

choices.text: A different metric for the Portuguese records
choices.why: An index has one metric, fixed at creation, for every record in it.

choices.text: Upserting the Portuguese vectors with smaller values
choices.why: Changing the numbers would only distort the ranking; it separates nothing.

choices.text: A namespace of their own, while English questions query only en
choices.why: Right. A query names one namespace and never sees the others, so forgetting a filter cannot leak them.
